name: Pascal's triangle
seoDesc: Pascal's triangle: a free math calculator that walks you through 4 values, with the formula spelled out and a worked example.
summary:
The Pascal's triangle calculator takes the values in the form and reports every result the relationship allows, with the formula and a worked example printed below. One number goes in, press Calculate, and the equivalent in the other unit appears; the factor that links them is printed below, so you can repeat the arithmetic yourself.

It is built for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Pascal's triangle calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pascal's triangle calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports show level in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the figures it asks for.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
What you supply, field by field
FieldUnits and meaning
Showpick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as the triangle up to... and only.... The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
Row...a plain number with no unit attached.

Both boxes accept a value, so it does not matter which one you start from. Type into the box you already know — the number in the other box is rewritten as soon as you press Calculate, and the unit chips beside them let you move to a third and fourth unit without leaving the page.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pascal's triangle calculator
sections.html:
This is a conversion rather than a calculation. Show level and row describe the same quantity, so the arithmetic underneath is a simple identity: whatever you type in one box is converted to a common base unit, and the other box is rendered from that base in its own unit.

That is why changing the unit chip does not change the underlying value, only the way it is written — and why you can enter a figure in either box and read the answer from the other.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pascal's triangle calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Pascal's triangle calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The 1 drop-down on this page offers a fixed list of cases. A value that is not on the list cannot be entered, and the nearest option is not always a good substitute.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — show... for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Pascal's triangle calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns show level. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pascal's triangle calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Pascal's triangle calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
